newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac, Jospin stress mutual respect.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac, Jospin stress mutual respect.

text.p: Conservative President Jacques Chirac and Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, launching a new era of power-sharing in France, promised on Thursday to work together to serve national interests.

"Here we are in a new period of 'cohabitation'," Chirac told the first meeting of Jospin's "Pink-Green-Red" cabinet that includes several women in senior posts, Communists for the first time since 1984, and a Green minister of the environment.

"I do not doubt that it will take place in a dignified manner with mutual respect and a constant concern for France's interests," he told the 26-strong government seated around an oval table in the gilded Elysee Palace.
The new period of cohabitation was the third in the history of France's Fifth Republic, which began in 1958, but the first between a left-wing prime minister and a right-wing head of state.

Jospin, who led the left's upset victory over Chirac's centre-right allies in Sunday's National Assembly election, said the 30-minute cabinet talks launching power-sharing went "well, very well". He said the tone was serious but relaxed.

The Paris Bourse saluted the broadly pro-European government, in which Communists hostile to a European single currency were confined to the transport and sports ministries. The CAC-40 blue chip stock index gained 2.11 percent on the day.
Chirac, who sat with a fixed smile when television cameras were briefly allowed in to film the meeting, stayed out of a cabinet photograph on the steps of the Elysee afterwards.
Jospin did not discuss his government's policy but promised to respect Chirac's prerogatives under the 1958 constitution, which gives the president a big role in foreign policy and defence.
The government focuses primarily on domestic policy, where the main challenge now is a record 12.8 percent unemployment rate.
After the cabinet meeting, the 59-year-old Jospin left for a first official trip abroad, going to the Swedish city of Malmo for a gathering of Socialist heads of government and parties.
He will address the conference on Friday and hold talks with Britain's new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn brushed off talk of German concern at the Socialists' attitude to the conditions for a single European currency. He told reporters after a handover with his predecessor: "There is no reason for Germany to be worried, so there is no reason for me to reassure them."
He said the new government's economic policy would couple change and continuity. "The French people wanted a new direction in policies," he said.

He said he would aim for a mix of "some of the policies which were pursued by our predecessors, which in part seem to us to be going in the right direction...and obviously some policy shifts will emerge."

Asked if the new government would try to renegotiate the so-called stability pact limiting EU member states' budget deficits after they join monetary union, junior European Affairs Minister Pierre Moscovici told reporters: "You'll see on Monday at the Ecofin".
Strauss-Kahn is due to attend his first meeting of EU economics and finance ministers in Luxembourg on Monday.
New Justice Minister Elisabeth Guigou said her first and most urgent task would be to restore citizens' confidence in the independence of the judicial system.

Judges have opened several investigations into politically charged cases this week, including illicit party funding, alleged rigged public tenders and illegal bugging, which had been on ice until after Sunday's parliamentary election runoff.

A court in Lyon gave former Socialist party leader Henri Emmanuelli an 18-month suspended prison sentence on Thursday for influence peddling in connection with a consultancy firm which channeled rake-offs from public works contracts to the party.

Chirac gambled disastrously by calling the election 10 months ahead of schedule, hoping his centre-right allies would win re-election to give him five clear years of conservative rule until his own seven-year term expires in 2002.
Instead, he is the greatly diminished prisoner of a hostile majority and his own Gaullist RPR party is in disarray.

Former parliament speaker Philippe Seguin, who led the 1992 campaign against the Maastricht treaty in France, formally announced his candidacy to succeed defeated prime minister Alain Juppe as RPR leader.
In the foreign policy realm, Jospin said he would attend a Franco-German summit in Poitiers, France, on June 13.

But in a sign of deference to Chirac, he would discuss participation at international summits with the president "in the interest of France and the state," according to Olivier Shrameck, head of Jospin's private office.
Major international meetings this month include a European Union summit in Amsterdam on June 16-17 and a summit of the Group of Seven nations in the U.S. city of Denver on June 20-22.
